bottlenecks.title: The verification tax
bottlenecks.body: The time a model saves is being spent back on checking its work — and the penalty for not checking has stopped being theoretical. Damien Charlotin's public database tracks roughly 1,490 court decisions worldwide where a party relied on AI-hallucinated material and a court responded, more than 1,000 of them US, running at more than one new decision per day. Penalties escalated from four-figure fines to $15,000 per attorney in a federal appeals court, an aggregate ~$109,700 across two lawyers in one matter, and the first suspensions: a Colorado attorney (a year and a day, 90 days to serve) and an indefinite suspension in Nebraska.

bottlenecks.title: Per-seat pricing against outcome value
bottlenecks.body: The deepest structural problem isn't capability, it's that the business model points the wrong way. Cut a five-hour task to one and billable revenue falls 80% while the work product is identical. Firms have mostly responded by not responding: 58% say AI has changed neither billing practices nor billable hours, 86% of solo and 78% of small firms haven't touched their pricing model, and only about a third report any associated revenue increase. Vendors have the mirror-image problem — seat licences priced against a value that is variable and outcome-shaped.

bottlenecks.title: Individuals adopted; institutions didn't
bottlenecks.body: Adoption among individual practitioners went 27% → 31% → 69% in three years. Firm-level adoption did not keep pace: 46% of firms have general-purpose AI tools and 34% have legal-specific ones (58% at firms of 21+ lawyers). The gap is shadow AI — the work is already being done on models the firm has not sanctioned, trained for, or insured against.

bottlenecks.title: The governance vacuum
bottlenecks.body: This is the one that turns into malpractice exposure. 43% of firms have no formal AI policy and no plans to write one; only 9% have a written policy that is actually enforced. 54% provide no AI training and have no plans to; only 11% make training mandatory. Every sanctions case above happened inside a firm that had, on these numbers, better-than-even odds of having no policy at all.

bottlenecks.title: Security, privilege and trust
bottlenecks.body: The stated blockers are remarkably consistent and they are not about accuracy: data security (46%), ethics (42%), privilege (39%) and lack of trust in outputs (39%), with cost a distant concern. This is why the model vendors' enterprise terms are doing real commercial work — OpenAI's Trusted Access (zero data retention, no human review, ethical walls designed with Latham) and Anthropic's enterprise posture are aimed squarely at this list rather than at benchmark scores.

bottlenecks.title: The data layer is an org chart problem
bottlenecks.body: Helen Fan's Level 3 — a system that learns from the work, inside agent, client and ethical-wall boundaries — is where defensibility actually lives, and it is the hardest crossing precisely because the blocker isn't technical. Somebody has to decide who owns which precedent, what a client's data may train, and how reader-writer separation maps onto information barriers. No vendor can sell a firm its way past that decision.

bottlenecks.title: Clients are ahead of their firms
bottlenecks.body: The demand-side pressure is inverting. 87% of GCs report using genAI in their teams, up from 44% a year earlier; corporate legal adoption more than doubled from 23% to 52%. 64% of in-house teams expect to depend less on outside counsel because of what they're building internally. And 60% don't know whether their firms use genAI on their matters at all — a disclosure gap that will close, on the client's terms.

bottlenecks.title: Regulation caps the best business model
bottlenecks.body: The AI-native firm — outcome pricing, AI first pass, lawyer as last checkpoint — needs non-lawyer ownership to take capital. In the US that is essentially Arizona's ABS programme and nowhere else. Every venture-scale AI-native firm is therefore structured around one state's rule, and UPL and fee-sharing rules elsewhere are a hard ceiling rather than a friction.

opportunities.title: Citation integrity as infrastructure
opportunities.body: A thousand US sanctions decisions is not a cautionary tale, it's a market signal. The gap is not better retrieval — it's court-defensible provenance: every proposition traceable to a verified source, with an audit artefact a judge or a malpractice carrier would accept. Midpage is closest in research; nobody owns it across drafting, and no carrier has productised it.

opportunities.title: Permissions-aware knowledge plumbing
opportunities.body: If Level 3 is the moat and the blocker is organisational, the buyable product is the thing that makes the organisational decision executable: ethical walls, reader-writer separation, per-client training consent, all enforced at retrieval time. DeepJudge, iManage and NetDocuments sit on this. Expect the platforms to buy here rather than build — it's the one asset a model vendor cannot ship from Ecosystems.

opportunities.title: Pricing and margin tooling
opportunities.body: 86% of small firms haven't changed pricing because nobody has given them a way to. Scoping an AFA, measuring realisation on a matter where a model did 80% of the work, and proving the saving to a client are all unserved. Manifest OS is the first real attempt and it raised the largest Series A in the sector's history — which tells you how empty the space is.

opportunities.title: Governance, training and attestation
opportunities.body: 43% of firms have no policy, 54% no training, and clients are about to start asking. That is a product, not a consulting engagement: policy generation against the firm's actual tool estate, enforced logging, mandatory training with completion records, and a client-facing attestation that survives an audit. It also happens to be what insurers will start pricing against.

opportunities.title: Client-facing AI and the disclosure gap
opportunities.body: 60% of in-house teams don't know whether their firms use genAI on their matters. Closing that gap is Helen Fan's 'client-facing AI' thesis — the firm exposes its AI work product and provenance to the client directly, which turns a transparency liability into the reason the client stays. Almost nobody is building the client-side surface for this.

opportunities.title: The long tail and the plaintiff bar
opportunities.body: Contingency firms buy on ROI, not headcount — which is why Eve, EvenUp and Filevine all crossed a billion in one autumn while BigLaw tools were still being piloted. The same logic applies to solo and small firms, where adoption is highest and tooling is priced for a market they aren't in. Clio owns the seat; almost nobody owns the AI layer on top of it.

opportunities.title: Primary law outside the US
opportunities.body: OpenAI's Legal Search Index is 230M+ URLs of US material. Anthropic's research connectors are US-weighted. Non-US and non-English primary law is substantially unbuilt at frontier quality — and the CourtListener precedent shows the data can come from public and nonprofit sources rather than from Westlaw or Lexis.

opportunities.title: A second ABS state
opportunities.body: The single highest-leverage event in the sector. If one more US state opens to non-lawyer ownership, the AI-native firm stops being Arizona regulatory arbitrage and becomes the default structure for commodity legal work — and every firm currently defending an hourly P&L has to re-underwrite its business at once.
